summary: Introduces and discusses issues in the design of accounting systems, which collect resource consumption data for capacity planning, cost allocation, auditing, and billing. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Accounting for a network means counting who used what, for planning and billing. This introduces what goes into that.

questions: how do you make accounting reliable
subtitle: Principles and design issues for collecting and managing resource consumption data.

tldr.problem: Network and IT organizations need to collect resource consumption data for capacity planning, cost allocation, auditing, and billing, but different applications have very different requirements for reliability, security, and speed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a taxonomy of accounting applications, their reliability and security requirements, and surveys existing protocols (RADIUS, TACACS+, SNMP) and data models to help system designers choose appropriate tools.
tldr.outcome: This informational guide helps organizations design accounting systems that meet their specific needs, from best-effort capacity planning to high-reliability billing systems.

facts.value: Capacity planning, billing, cost allocation, auditing

facts.label: Key reliability issue
facts.value: Non-volatile storage is more important than transport protocol choice

facts.label: Data collection models
facts.value: Polling, event-driven (with or without batching), and hybrid

today: RFC 2975 remains the authoritative framework for understanding accounting system design and trade-offs. It has not been obsoleted. Most accounting deployments still use RADIUS or variants, though modern systems increasingly use DIAMETER (RFC 6733) and other protocols for advanced requirements.

sections.title: Introduction to Accounting Management
sections.content:
Accounting management is the collection of resource consumption data for capacity planning, trend analysis, cost allocation, auditing, and billing. The RFC notes that different accounting applications have different requirements: a capacity planner can tolerate moderate packet loss, while a billing system may have legal and financial requirements for near-perfect reliability. Since no single protocol can meet all needs, the goal is to provide a set of tools for each application.

This document describes the problems that accounting systems solve, design issues in modern accounting systems, and reviews existing tools (RADIUS accounting, TACACS+, SNMP). A companion document, RFC 2924, reviews accounting attributes and record formats.
sections.eli5: Different organizations need to count different things with different levels of care. Some care if they miss a bit of data; others must catch every byte for billing accuracy.

sections.title: Accounting Objectives and Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four main objectives for accounting data collection. Trend analysis and capacity planning forecast future usage and tolerate moderate packet loss. Billing ranges from non-usage-sensitive (flat fees, where data loss is less critical) to usage-sensitive (per-minute or per-byte charges, requiring high reliability). Auditing verifies invoice correctness and conformance to policy, requiring reliability and security at least as stringent as billing.

Cost allocation distributes known costs across departments or entities, typically usage-sensitive and requiring archival accounting reliability due to financial and legal requirements. The RFC notes that requirements also differ between intra-domain (within one organization, lower packet loss) and inter-domain (crossing organizational boundaries, higher packet loss) accounting. Usage-sensitive billing and cost allocation often require archival accounting—techniques to survive server failures, reboots, and network outages by storing records in non-volatile storage.
sections.eli5: Counting for planning is easy; counting for billing is hard. Counting when you're talking to another company is harder. And counting for legal reasons (audits, cost allocation) is the hardest.

sections.title: Fault Resilience and Reliability
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four major fault types: packet loss, accounting server failures, network failures, and device reboots. It argues that non-volatile storage is the single most important reliability mechanism—without it, devices will lose data once retransmission timeouts expire or internal buffers fill. Transport choice (UDP, TCP, or SCTP) does not affect resilience against server outages or network partitions; only non-volatile storage does.

Interim accounting provides checkpoints during a session that can reconstruct the session record if the final summary is lost. However, interim data transmitted over the wire increases bandwidth consumption and is most useful for long-lived sessions stored in non-volatile memory. Duplicate elimination, application-layer acknowledgments (rather than relying only on transport-layer ACKs), and accounting proxies that pass through acknowledgments rather than store-and-forward all contribute to reliability. The RFC warns that store-and-forward proxies can actually reduce overall reliability if the proxy itself becomes a single point of failure.
sections.eli5: Save your data to a hard drive so you don't lose it if the power fails. Send important data in pieces (checkpoints) so you can rebuild if something breaks in the middle. And make sure you know the counting system actually worked, not just that the data arrived.

sections.title: Resource Consumption and Data Collection Models
sections.content:
Accounting systems consume network bandwidth, memory, non-volatile storage, CPU, and require state management. The RFC discusses efficiency measures: batching and compression reduce bandwidth; compression and interim accounting overwrite reduce memory; per-device state (rather than per-session) reduces system state; and hardware-assisted compression and encryption reduce CPU load.

Four data collection models are surveyed. The polling model (manager periodically requests data from devices) scales with the number of devices and is efficient for data transfer, but introduces latency and does not work well for roaming or shared services. The event-driven model without batching (device reports each event separately) offers low latency for real-time applications like fraud detection but is inefficient and scales poorly. The event-driven model with batching (device sends events when a batch accumulates) balances efficiency and latency. The event-driven polling model combines elements of both for flexibility.
sections.eli5: You can ask devices periodically what happened (polling), or you can have devices call you when something important happens (event-driven). Collecting events in batches is more efficient than reporting one by one.

sections.title: Accounting Protocols and Data Transfer
sections.content:
The RFC briefly surveys three existing protocols. RADIUS accounting is the most widely deployed accounting protocol, using UDP-based transport with application-layer reliability. It is sufficient for intra-domain accounting and best-effort capacity planning but limited for high-reliability applications due to its UDP base and simple attribute design. TACACS+ is a proprietary protocol (less commonly deployed) using TCP and supporting more sophisticated authentication and authorization. SNMP can be used for accounting but is primarily a management protocol.

For data transfer, the RFC notes that protocols like SMTP or custom transfer protocols may be used to submit accounting records to billing systems, but most real-time accounting uses RADIUS or similar protocols. The RFC emphasizes that no single protocol meets all needs; organizations should choose based on their specific reliability, security, and performance requirements.
sections.eli5: RADIUS is the standard tool for reporting accounting data. It works pretty well but has some limitations. Stronger tools exist for critical billing systems.
